description: We are from Jacobabad, Sindh, one of the hottest places on Earth. Our challenge is Be An Earth System Trend Detective. We are using NASA data to show rising heat and its impact on farming, water and health in our area. We have skills in graphic design, research and storytelling and learning data analysis for our project.
summary:
Jacobabad Climate Monitor is a web-based tool that uses live NASA POWER data to show how extreme heat affects Jacobabad, Pakistan, one of the hottest cities on Earth.

Our dashboard compares Jacobabad with Karachi and Lahore using real daily temperature data from 2015 to 2026. It shows that Jacobabad had 738 days above 45°C, while Lahore had 170 and Karachi had 0. It also shows an upward trend of +0.28°C per decade and explains what this heat means for outdoor workers, children, older adults, and farmers.

We do not just show data. We propose a low-cost, local solution: the Jacobabad Cool Spine & Solar Shade Network, with solar shade, cool roofs, native trees, heat-relief stops, and community sensors.

This project makes NASA data simple, local, and useful for people who face extreme heat every summer.
details:
Jacobabad Climate Monitor is a web dashboard that uses live NASA POWER data to make extreme heat visible and understandable for Jacobabad, Pakistan.

What does it do and how does it work?

The user opens the dashboard and selects a city: Jacobabad, Karachi, or Lahore. The dashboard fetches real data from the NASA POWER API for 2015 to 2026. It shows latest conditions, annual maximum temperature trend, city comparison, and number of days above 45°C. It also shows a recent daily temperature graph. All charts update from real NASA data, not from manual estimates.

What are the benefits and intended impact?

People in Jacobabad feel extreme heat but do not have simple local proof. Our tool gives them that proof. It shows Jacobabad had 738 days above 45°C from 2015 to 2026, while Lahore had 170 and Karachi had 0. It shows a trend of +0.28°C per decade. This helps students, workers, farmers, and local leaders understand risk and plan shade, water, and rest during heatwaves.

What tools did we use?

We used NASA POWER API, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and http://Chart.js for charts. Parameters used: T2M, T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN, RH2M, PRECTOTCORR, WS10M. We used Google Slides for demonstration and GitHub / Netlify for hosting.

How is it creative?

We did not just show graphs. We connected NASA data to human life: health, work, water, and farming. We also proposed a low-cost local solution: Jacobabad Cool Spine & Solar Shade Network, with solar shade, cool roofs, native trees, heat-relief stops, and community sensors. We were honest about limitations: NASA POWER is gridded satellite data, not a street thermometer, and our trend is descriptive, not proof of causation.

Our goal is simple: make NASA data local, simple, and useful for people who live in extreme heat.
